(InStyle.com) -- It takes a truly adventurous actress to pull off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie and a Louise Brooks bob, but we'd expect nothing less from the ever provocative Selma Blair, who experimented with all three looks in under a year. Selma Blair says she works with hairstylists and makeup artists who "have a vision." "I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes," proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC's upcoming mom-and-daughter sitcom "Kath and Kim" and July's action flick "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-declared "poor applier," who sticks with basics like nude lipstick and pink blush, and ducks whenever she sees a liquid liner. "I avoid anything difficult," she says. Blair's signature look: "A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara--I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!" Have you always been a beauty chameleon? In high school I would mess with my hair and makeup all the time. I used to wear a shirt that said "Ms. Clairol" because I changed my hair color so much. I was blond for a long time, then what my mom called "barnyard red." Do you still dye it yourself? Only when I have to cover up stray grays. And I'll just use whatever color I find in the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Preference by L'Oréal--because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to very slowly strip out all the color so that my hair wouldn't burn off. And the cut--are you keeping it short? I tend to like my hair whatever way it's not, so now I miss it being long. I think I'm more approachable with long hair. When it's short, I come across as being artsy and weird. What's your typical makeup look? I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and when I got a pimple, I'd cover it up with eyeliner to turn it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I hit 35. I'm at an age where any makeup that's meant to look "slept in" really looks like I slept in it. That's for youngsters! Now less is more. I don't like to wear concealer or anything. I'd rather have uneven skin than feel like my face is cracking from too much foundation. Then you must be serious about your skin care. I go to a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions and they'll look at your skin and tell you how to get it in better condition. They really helped me a lot. I also stay out of the sun. Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery? I wanted to get Botox once to make me feel younger. But I don't really have [enough wrinkles] to justify it yet. As for going under the knife, I can't say I wouldn't, but I haven't thought too much about it. Best beauty product? Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works for my friend's baby's bottom, and I can also use it instead of Chapstick. So what's next? I'm really excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long highlighted hair extensions for my role on "Kath and Kim." And I've been gaining weight for the part by eating a little bit more of what I want and not moving around as much. I've already put on 15 pounds, and I'll probably gain another 10. It'll be a whole new me! Will this be your most drastic transformation? Actually I wore huge prosthetic boobs for a John Waters movie. They were glued on every day by a really handsome guy, but ripping them off every night was definitely outside my realm of comfort. After those bosoms, I didn't mind being flat-chested anymore! Louise sat in the plush leather chair of *Atelier Nova*, lazily flipping through the crisp, glossy pages of *InStyle* magazine. The issue was filled with fall trends: camel coats, tailored trousers, and soft, cascading waves. For years, Louise had adhered strictly to that exact aesthetic. As a senior art director at an advertising firm, her style was polished, predictable, and undeniably safe.

But today, looking at the neatly curated spread in front of her, she felt a sudden surge of restlessness. 

"So, the usual touch-up and blow-dry today, Louise?" asked Marco, her stylist of six years, adjusting the cape around her neck.

Louise looked at her reflection in the gilded mirror. She saw a woman who had played by the rules for too long. She looked back down at the magazine, then closed it with a decisive *snap*, setting it on the coffee table beside her.

"No," Louise said, her voice steady. "Not today. I want you to shave the sides."

Marco paused, his scissors hovering in mid-air. "Shave? Like a undercut?"

"No," Louise smiled, a flash of thrill washing over her. "A Mohawk. A sleek, modern, platinum-blonde Mohawk."

Marco’s eyes widened, but a slow, excited grin spread across his face. "Now *that* is a statement."

For the next two hours, the buzz of the clippers replaced the soft jazz playing in the salon. Strands of Louise’s mouse-brown hair fell to the floor like discarded layers of an old identity. Marco bleached the remaining strip of hair to a striking, ice-cold platinum, styling it into a textured, elegant ridge that tapered perfectly at the nape of her neck.

When he finally spun the chair around, Louise caught her breath. The transformation was fierce. The sharp contrast of the Mohawk brought out the structure of her cheekbones and the intensity of her eyes. It was edgy, yet oddly sophisticated—less punk rock garage band, more haute couture runway.

She picked up the copy of *InStyle* off the table, holding it next to her reflection. She realized then that true style wasn't about blindly following the pages of a magazine; it was about the confidence to write your own narrative. 

Louise tipped her head, admired the sharp line of her new cut, and walked out into the city streets, ready to be seen.

### **InStyle Magazine (2008) – Selma Blair: Beauty Secrets**

**InStyle:** *You’ve bounced between long hair, bobs, and pixie cuts over the years. How do you feel about your short hair right now?*

**Selma Blair:** "I love short hair. It is so liberating. When my hair is short, I feel more like myself—it brings out your features in a way long hair sometimes hides. Plus, the routine is minimal: you wash it, throw in a little texturizing pomade or serum to keep it piecy, and walk out the door. It takes five minutes."

**InStyle:** *You are famous for embracing your pale complexion rather than faking a tan. Was that a conscious choice?*

**Selma Blair:** "Definitely. Early on, people in Hollywood would tell you to get a spray tan or sit in the sun, but it just didn’t look right on me. I’m naturally very fair. Once I accepted it, it became my signature. Pale skin looks gorgeous when it’s healthy and hydrated. The key is just accepting your natural tone and protecting it."

**InStyle:** *What is your daily skincare philosophy?*

**Selma Blair:** "Sunscreen is non-negotiable. I wear a heavy sunblock every single day, no matter what the weather is doing outside. Aside from that, I keep it simple: a gentle cleanser, a rich moisturizer at night, and lots of rosewater spray during the day to keep my skin looking fresh and dewy."

---

### **In Her Makeup Bag (2008 Feature Callouts)**

During the 2008 *InStyle* spread, Selma shared her daily go-to products that created her signature look:

* **The Holy Grail Concealer:** *Clé de Peau Beauté Concentrated Concealer* 
  > *"It covers everything—dark circles, redness—without looking cakey on pale skin."*
* **The Classic Red Lip:** *MAC Lip Pencil in Cherry paired with classic red lipstick* 
  > *"If I’m going out and don't want to do a full face of makeup, a strong red lip is all I need."*
* **The Flush:** *Stila Convertible Color Dual Lip & Cheek Cream* 
  > *"A tiny dab on the apples of the cheeks gives that natural, 'just walked in from the cold' flush."*
* **Hair Styling:** *Kérastase Nutritive Serum / Bumble and bumble Sumotech* 
  > *"Essential for keeping short hair looking chic rather than messy."*

---

### **Selma’s Top Beauty Rules (from the 2008 Interview)**

1. **Focus on One Feature:** *"If I’m doing a dark, dramatic eye, I keep my lips completely nude. If I wear a bold red lip, I just do mascara and clean skin. Doing both at once feels too done-up for me."*
2. **Don't Fight Your Hair Texture:** *"The moment you stop trying to force your hair to do something it naturally hates, your mornings get an hour shorter."*
3. **Hydration Over Everything:** *"If your skin is dry, no makeup in the world is going to look good on top of it. Hydrate first, makeup second."*

**Beauty Talk: Selma Blair on Her Wild Hair History, Gaining Weight for *Kath & Kim*, and the $39 Miracle Cream She Can’t Live Without**

*By InStyle Staff | October 2008*

Selma Blair has never been one to play it safe. Whether she’s rocking a razor-sharp raven bob, a bleached-blonde pixie, or a graphic designer outfit on the red carpet, the 36-year-old actress is a beauty chameleon in the truest sense. 

Currently preparing for the premiere of NBC’s highly anticipated comedy *Kath & Kim*—in which she plays Kim, the suburban, velour-tracksuit-loving daughter to Molly Shannon’s Kath—Blair sat down with *InStyle.com* to talk about her wildest mane moments, her very lazy beauty routine, and why she welcomed a few extra pounds for her newest role.

***

**InStyle.com: You are absolute royalty when it comes to dramatic hair transformations. Looking back, which style was the wildest for you?**

**Selma Blair:** Oh gosh, where do we start? I have zero patience, which is why I’m always cutting my hair off or changing the color. I loved my platinum pixie, but I think the absolute wildest was when I did a short, razored Mohawk a few years back. My hair stylist was probably terrified, but I just said, "Take it off!" I’ve had it black, bright yellow-blonde, long, shaved... honestly, hair grows back! It’s just hair. Though I will say, bleaching it until your scalp feels like it’s on fire is something I try to avoid these days. 

**InStyle.com: For your new show, *Kath & Kim*, you have a pretty memorable look—lots of hair extensions and very questionable suburban fashion.**

**SB:** [Laughs] Kim’s style is… an homage to acrylics, spray tans, and hair extensions that don't quite blend. It’s glorious. I wear these terrible cropped tracksuits with words written across the butt. It is the absolute opposite of how I dress in real life, which made it an absolute dream to play.

**InStyle.com: Is it true you actually gained weight for the role of Kim?**

**SB:** I did! Kim is someone who constantly eats junk food and thinks she’s a total supermodel regardless. So the producers said, "You can put on some weight," and I was like, "Say no more!" I stopped holding back. I ate the bread basket, I ate the doughnuts. I probably gained about seven or eight pounds, which on my frame shows up. And honestly? It was liberating. In Hollywood, women spend so much time trying to shrink. To be told to eat a pancake was heaven. Plus, it helped fill out Kim’s tight little Juicy Couture tracksuits just right.

**InStyle.com: Off-camera, your skin always looks naturally glowing and fresh. What does your everyday beauty routine look like?**

**SB:** It’s ridiculously low-maintenance because I’m inherently lazy. I don't do ten steps. But I have one secret weapon that I’m obsessed with: Egyptian Magic cream. Someone gave me a tub of it years ago on a movie set, and I’ve been addicted ever since. It’s this olive oil and honey balm, and I slather it everywhere. I put it on my face at night, on my cuticles, on dry elbows, on my lips, even on the ends of my hair if it’s feeling fried. It’s cheap, it lasts forever, and it just works.

**InStyle.com: What about makeup? Are you a full-face girl when you leave the house?**

**SB:** Absolutely not. If I’m not working or doing a red carpet, I wear almost nothing. A little bit of concealer under the eyes—because I naturally look like a Victorian ghost—a swipe of mascara, and lip balm. Maybe a smudge of dark eyeliner if I’m trying to look a little rock ’n’ roll for dinner. I think the older I get, the less makeup I actually want on my face. Heavy foundation just sits in places you don't want it to.

**InStyle.com: You turned 36 this year. How are you feeling about aging in an industry that’s notoriously obsessed with youth?**

**SB:** You know, in my twenties, I was so filled with anxiety and self-doubt. Now that I’m in my thirties, I feel so much more comfortable in my own skin. Sure, you see a little line here or a spot there, but I’m okay with it. Aging means you’ve lived, you’ve laughed, you’ve survived a few bad haircuts! I look at women like Lauren Hutton or Meryl Streep, and they are so stunning because they have character in their faces. I don't want to erase my history. I just want to keep laughing, keep changing my hair whenever I get bored, and keep putting Egyptian Magic on my face.

### **MAGAZINE ARCHIVE: *ALLURE* / JULY 2008**

# BEAUTY DOS & DON'TS WITH SELMA BLAIR
*By Sarah Connelly*

Whether she’s rocking a bleached-blonde pixie cut or raven-black finger waves, Selma Blair, 36, is Hollywood’s ultimate beauty chameleon. We sat down with the *Hellboy II* star to talk home hair dye disasters, her holy-grail skincare secret, and the $8 drugstore staple she can’t live without.

***

**ALLURE:** You’ve bounced between platinum blonde, chocolate brown, and jet-black over the years. What’s your natural hair color at this point?
**SELMA BLAIR:** [Laughs] Honestly, I think my natural color is "mousy dishwater," but I haven’t seen it since 1994. Right now, I’m back to my signature dark shade. I just feel more like *me* when I’m dark. When I’m blonde, I feel like I’m wearing a costume, but dark hair instantly gives me a confidence boost. 

**ALLURE:** Do you ever dye it yourself, or are you strictly a salon girl?
**SELMA:** Oh, I am terrible—I’m a total home-dyer. I know my colorist hates me for it, but if I see a stray gray or I’m bored on a Sunday night, I’ll just run to CVS, grab a box of dark brown or black dye, and do it in my bathroom sink. The trick is using a gloss treatment right after—like the Kérastase Chroma Reflect—otherwise box dye can look flat. But yeah, my towels are all permanently stained dark brown.

**ALLURE:** You are famous for your flawless, pale skin. In an era where everyone in LA is spray-tanned orange, how do you embrace the porcelain look?
**SELMA:** I tried the fake tan thing once in the early 2000s and I looked like an Oompa Loompa. Never again! I realized early on that I’m never going to be a golden beach babe, so I embraced the Snow White vibe. My biggest rule is sunblock, every single day. I love Neutrogena Ultra Sheer Dry-Touch SPF 55—it doesn't break me out under camera makeup, and it keeps me totally pale. 

**ALLURE:** Walk us through your daily skincare routine. Are you a minimalist or a 10-step person?
**SELMA:** Totally minimalist. I wash my face with good old-fashioned Cetaphil Gentle Skin Cleanser. It’s boring, but it works. Then I slather on Crème de la Mer. It’s an absolute fortune, but my skin just drinks it up, especially after long days on movie sets under hot lights. If I get a breakout, I use Mario Badescu Drying Lotion overnight. It looks ridiculous—you end up with pink dots all over your face—but it dries a spot up in hours.

**ALLURE:** What’s always inside your makeup bag right now?
**SELMA:** I don’t wear a ton of foundation on my day off. I just use Yves Saint Laurent Touche Éclat under my eyes—it’s magic in a gold pen. Then I swipe on NARS Orgasm blush because it gives you that "I just went for a run" flush. For lips, I’m obsessed with Smith’s Rosebud Salve. I have a tin of it in every purse, my car, and my coat pocket. 

**ALLURE:** Who is your ultimate beauty icon?
**SELMA:** Judy Garland, Audrey Hepburn, and Edie Sedgwick. Women who understood dramatic eyes and didn't try to look like everyone else. Beauty should be a little bit fun and a little bit dramatic.

---

### **Media Studies Context & Analysis (Why this fits 2008):**

If you are analyzing this for a project, notice these specific late-2000s beauty media conventions present in the text:

1. **The "High-Low" Product Mix:** 2000s magazines loved pairing extremely expensive luxury items (Crème de la Mer at ~$250/jar) with accessible drugstore products (Cetaphil, Neutrogena, Rosebud Salve). This made celebrities feel relatable yet aspirational.
2. **Specific "Cult-Favorite" Product Mentions:** Products like *NARS Orgasm Blush*, *YSL Touche Éclat*, and *Mario Badescu Drying Lotion* were ubiquitous in almost every celebrity beauty Q&A between 2005 and 2010. 
3. **The Anti-Tanning Shift:** By 2008, the heavy "Paris Hilton/Britney Spears" bronzed tan look of the early 2000s was fading, replaced by a trend emphasizing pale, protected skin (driven partly by celebrities like Selma Blair, Anne Hathaway, and Dita Von Teese).
4. **Self-Deprecating Tone:** The framing of the star as "relatable" (staining her towels with box dye) was a key editing choice used by magazines to break the wall between Hollywood stars and readers.
